chunks: What is pipelining?. The question: What is pipelining?
Pipelining means starting the next instruction before the previous one has finished. The work of an instruction is split into stages, with a register between each pair of stages.
Each stage then works on a different instruction at the same time. A single instruction takes no less time, but instructions finish at a much higher rate.
Picture a car assembly line. One station fits the engine, the next the doors, the next the wheels. At any moment, several cars are being built, each at a different station.
A finished car rolls off each time the slowest station finishes its job.
Building one car from start to end takes no less time, and a bit more, but the factory produces far more cars per day.
The solid curve flattens at 3. 33, well under the dashed ideal limit of 5.
The gap is stage imbalance (MEM 250 picoseconds vs 180 picoseconds average) and the 20 picoseconds register overhead.
Even the ideal curve only approaches 5 slowly because of the fill time.
Stage: one slice of the instruction's work that fits in one clock cycle. Pipeline register: storage between stages that holds each instruction's in-progress data.
Throughput: how many instructions finish per second. Latency: how long one instruction takes from start to finish.
Hazard: a dependency that stops the next instruction from going ahead on schedule ("The five-stage pipeline").
Use the page's five stages, which take 200, 150, 200, 250 and 100 picoseconds, plus 20 picoseconds of register overhead.
Without pipelining, one instruction takes 900 picoseconds, so one finishes every 900 picoseconds.
With pipelining, the clock must fit the slowest stage plus overhead: 250 + 20 = 270 picoseconds. Now one instruction finishes every 270 picoseconds, about 3.
3 times the throughput. But one instruction's own trip is 5 times 270 = 1350 picoseconds, which is longer than 900 picoseconds.
That is the whole idea: higher throughput, same or worse latency.
"Pipelining splits an instruction's work into stages separated by registers so several instructions are in flight at once, each in a different stage.
The clock only has to cover the slowest stage instead of the whole path, so you get a much higher clock and, once full, roughly one instruction per cycle.
Latency for a single instruction doesn't improve, it gets slightly worse, so it's a throughput win.
The speedup is less than the number of stages because of register overhead, unbalanced stages and hazards like data dependencies and branches."
